 What to know about portable power stations
 Capacity (Wh) vs. Output (Watts): Each portable power station comes with a capacity rating in Wh and an output rating in W. The Wh refers to the station's total capacity when it's fully charged, while the W explains its maximum output at any given time. Models with larger Wh and W can handle high-draw appliances and HVAC systems.
 Power Stations vs. Gas Generators: Both power stations and gas generators are great options for home power backup. Gas generators are easy to operate and provide unlimited power as long as the tank is filled with fuel. If you'd rather have home backup that's quiet in operation and safe to use indoors, a portable power station is the better option.
 Why Size Matters: Buying a portable power station that's too small for your needs could leave you stranded with uncharged devices. Buying a model that's too big could mean spending more money than necessary or ending up with a heavy station you avoid pulling out to use. Here's a quick guide to finding the right size for your needs.
 Under 500Wh : Best for recharging small devices during a short outage. Under 500Wh is perfect for keeping phones, tablets, and earbuds charged up during a weekend camping or a power outage lasting a couple of days. This size is also highly portable, making it perfect for carrying from room to room in the house during a power cut.
 1,000Wh—2,000Wh: Something in the 1,000Wh to 2,000Wh range gives you enough power to keep small devices charged as well as use some kitchen appliances like the coffee machine and lights. 2,000 Wh is also sufficient to keep the refrigerator running during an outage for up to two days.
 3,000Wh+: Over 3,000Wh gives you plenty of power to keep your home powered up if the grid fails. You can keep the refrigerator plugged in, run lights, run the air purifier, keep the WiFi router powered up, recharge phones, and even whiz a smoothie in the blender.
 Solar Integration: Almost every modern portable power station can recharge via solar panels. Recharging with a solar panel is especially useful if you live in an area that sees plenty of sunny days or you'll be taking a portable power station camping in the summer. Before you buy, check each station's solar compatibility and the maximum solar wattage it can handle. Smaller power stations might only be able to connect up to 100W of solar, while larger stations can handle 3,000W of solar input.

 Portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV , or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely. They’re effectively large bundles of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which provide a quiet, exhaust-free alternative to noisy gas-powered portable generators .
 Portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow , including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout . Plus, most can be recharged using solar panels .

 How We Tested
 We evaluated eight power stations of varying size, focusing on each model’s maximum output, capacity, charging time, and portability. To test max output, we connected enough electronics and appliances to each power station to meet or slightly exceed their listed max output to see how well they could operate at maximum load. We then tested capacity, using an electricity usage monitor to record the total watt-hours each power station produced while running them under a consistent load.
 Once they were drained, we charged each power station from 0 to 100 percent using their AC adapters, timing how long it took to get to 80 and 100 percent capacity. Finally, we evaluated each power station’s portability by attempting to carry it or roll it. Other factors that weighed into our decisions included the number and power output of each power station’s inputs and its charging options.

And while the F3800 is one of the heavier models we’ve tested, weighing over 135 pounds, its upright suitcase-like design and four sturdy wheels made it easier to wheel around our homes than other large power stations with two wheels and a handle. And with a small footprint, we were able to store it out of the way in a busy kitchen by tucking it into a corner. (Another option is to lay it down into a horizontal position, which is useful for RVs.)
 The Anker F3800 Plus is loaded with six AC ports (most power stations have just four). That allowed us to load it up with various appliances and power tools without having to use a power strip. There’s also an RV port for campers, and a 240-volt port for larger appliances such as an oven or dryer.

 What to Consider
 Maximum Output
 A portable power station’s maximum output tells you the total watts it can produce, which determines what you can and can’t power with it. Look for a power station that can handle the combined wattage of the electronics you plan to plug into it.
 Some power stations also have surge power that allows them to produce higher wattage for short bursts. This is designed specifically for appliances that draw more watts (known as starting watts) in the first few seconds that you first start them up, including power tools, refrigerators, blenders, and window air conditioners.
 Capacity
 A portable power station’s capacity, listed in watt-hours (Wh), determines how much energy a power station can deliver over time. Generally, power stations with more watt-hours can run for longer, but exactly how long depends on the amount of watts the devices connected to the power station draw. You can roughly estimate how long a power station will last by dividing the total watt-hours by the watts drawn (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).
 For example, if you have a power station with 2,048 watt-hour capacity, and are consistently drawing 400 watts of power: 2,048 ÷ 400 = 5.12 hours of runtime.
 Keep in mind that the usable watt hours are not the same as the watt hours listed on the power station’s label. You’ll typically get about 85 percent of the listed watt-hours due to power lost in connections and the electricity that the power station itself uses to power its inverter and display. Given those losses, expect to get about 85 percent of a power station’s listed watt-hours in usable power. So, a fully charged 2,000-watt-hour power station will typically give you about 1,700 watt-hours of usable power.
 Battery Technology
 These days, most portable power stations, including all those we recommend here, use LiFePO4 batteries, which are capable of holding far more cycles, which is the number of times a battery goes through a complete discharge and recharge, than older lithium-ion batteries, while also being less likely to combust. Their one drawback is that they have a lower energy density, which means it takes more LiFePO4 batteries than lithium-ion batteries to produce the same amount of power. Still, this is the battery type of choice for portable power stations, both large and small.
 Portability
 While all these power stations are portable, some are easier to transport than others. A power station’s portability is directly related to its power capacity and output.
 Small power stations with around 300 watt-hours of capacity and a max output of 300 watts, such as the Anker Solix C300 DC portable power station , typically weigh under 10 pounds and are about the size of a lunch box.
 Mid-size models like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 portable power station , which have a max wattage of between 2,000 and 2,600 watts and a 2,000-watt-hour capacity, are about the size of the printer in your home office and weigh around 60 pounds, just small and light enough for one person to carry from one room to another.
 Large portable models such as the EcoFlow Pro Delta 3 , which can sustain a max output of up to 6,000 watts with a 4,000-watt-hour capacity, can weigh up to 135 pounds and are about the size of a suitcase. While these monsters are too large for one person to lift, they do sit on wheels that allow you to move them over flat surfaces, technically making them portable.
 Ports
 Portable power stations have an array of output ports, including USB-C, USB-A, car accessory, AC, and RV. Consider what types of appliances or electronics you’re planning to charge and the type of connections they use when choosing a portable power station.
 Since the wattage of the output can vary, also consider the maximum charging output of each port to avoid disappointing recharge times. For example, a power station with a USB-C port that has a 15-watt max output will take a much longer time to charge a laptop than one with a 140-watt USB-C port.
 If you’re looking for a large capacity power station that will backup critical circuits in your home or power an RV, you’ll need a station that features a single 30-amp connection that can connect to an RV input or transfer switch.
 Controls
 Portable power stations have control panels with LED displays and buttons that turn off and on inputs and display usage and remaining power. Most portable power stations are also compatible with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, allowing you to monitor and control them remotely from a smartphone app.
 Often, what makes a power station great is the kind of software it includes and what features it offers to help you best manage your power station. For example, some stations that you leave plugged into a wall—so that it stays charged and at the ready—will automatically only recharge your station during low-peak hours when rates may be lower from your electric utility. Features like this one can be incredibly helpful when trying to get the most from your station.
 UPS
 Most large power stations, including the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus and Anker F3800 Plus, can serve as an UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your home. To use these power stations as a UPS, plug them into the wall, then plug whatever devices you want backed up into the station’s AC output ports. When the power is on, those devices use energy from the grid. When there is a power outage, the power station instantly switches these devices to battery power. If you live in an area prone to power outages, thus can be useful to prevent data loss from a connected computer, keep medical devices running, or even the pump and filter on a fish tank.
 Noise
 Portable power stations heat up when operating for extended periods or when they’re providing power for multiple devices. Internal fans will kick on to keep the power station from overheating. While these fans are far quieter than the roar of a gas-powered generator, they do still create some noise. Smaller power stations are about as loud as a small fan, while larger ones produce about the same amount of noise as a refrigerator.

 FAQs
 How long do portable power stations last? 
 A portable power station’s lifespan depends on the type of battery inside. Most new portable power stations, including all the models we recommend here, feature LiFePO4 battery technology, which lasts far longer than older lithium-ion technology.
 How much more? LiFePO4 power stations will last for more than 3,000 charge cycles, or about 10 years. That’s far longer than the 500 or so charge cycles and 3 to 5 years you’ll get from an older power station with a lithium-ion battery.
 How long does it take to recharge a portable power station with solar panels? 
 That depends on the capacity of your portable power station, the wattage of your solar panels, and the weather. To figure that out, divide the station’s total capacity by the total input power of the solar panels (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).
 For example, a 1,000-watt-hour power station that’s receiving a consistent stream of 200 watts of power from a solar panel would take about 5 hours to recharge. Keep in mind, this is assuming uninterrupted, direct sunlight conditions, which, even then, may produce varied results.
 Are portable power stations weather-resistant? 
 Some power stations have ingress protection (IP) ratings, indicating they have been tested for water and dust resistance. The Bluetti Elite 200, for example, has an IP65 rating, which means it can withstand water sprays from all angles. However, other portable power stations do not have a weather rating, so it’s important to check if you plan on using your power station outdoors. Regardless, it’s a good idea to protect your power station from any water or severe weather conditions as much as possible.

 Which makers have Black Friday sales in 2026?
 All four big makers now have dated sales, and all four end on November 18. Expect a second round for Black Friday week.
 EcoFlow: Early Black Friday sale from 12:00 AM PDT November 2 to 11:59 PM PDT November 18, “up to 52% off,” with member prices.  Jackery: Black Friday sale November 4 to 18. Triple points on purchases from November 4 to December 6, a $200-off coupon when you first register as a member, and a draw for subscribers to win an order free (up to $2,000). The cart mentions a 30-day price match, but the sale page gives no terms.

 How to tell a real power station deal from a fake one
 A real deal is one that beats the recent low, not the crossed-out number. Crossed-out prices on these sites rarely tell you much. Three checks take a minute:
 Work out the price per watt-hour. Divide the price by the capacity in watt-hours. On this page, anything under $0.40 is unusual, and anything over $0.70 needs a reason, such as 240V, expansion or extra output.
 Compare with a recent price. Use our table above. A $200 off badge means little if the price was lower last month, as with the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2.
 Check the cart. Anker showed $699.99 and $999.99 for the S2000 on the same day, and Jackery’s 2000 v2 page said “$0 OFF” under a Black Friday banner. Trust the price at checkout, and take a screenshot.
 Should you buy a solar bundle on Black Friday?
 Buy one if you know you need panels, because a bundle usually costs less than buying them apart. Anker’s S2000 with a 400W panel is $1,199.99, only $500 more than the station alone, though that bundle ships from early December. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 with a 200W panel is $699, $200 more than the unit. Check the station’s maximum solar input first: the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 takes 400W according to our review, so a bigger panel gives you more than it can use.
 Skip the bundle if your outages last hours rather than days, because you may never unfold the panels. Our guide to portable power stations vs generators helps you work out how long an outage you are planning for.
 How we chose these Black Friday power stations
 We picked units we have already researched from the biggest makers selling on their own US sites, from 1 kWh to 4 kWh, and looked up the same units on November 2 and November 12. We left out retailers such as Amazon, Home Depot and Costco, because we only quote prices from the seller’s own site, so a lower price may exist elsewhere. Our picks are roughly ordered by how good the current price is, not by how good the product is. For that, see our best portable power station for home backup list and our picks for the best portable power station under $1,000 .
 How to choose the right Black Friday power station
 Start with what you want to run. Add up the watts of everything you want on at the same time, then choose a unit with at least that much output. Our guide to what size power station you need for a refrigerator shows the math for the most common load.
 Then pick a size. A 1 kWh unit covers a night of essentials, and a 2 kWh unit lasts about twice as long. If you need 240V or several circuits, look at our best whole home battery backup list and budget for an electrician. Our guide on how to connect a power station to your house explains the options.
 Buy for stock, not just price. On November 12, four of the eight units here were sold out and two more ship in December. If you need power for winter storms, an in-stock unit at a slightly higher price beats a lower price that arrives after the storm.
 Who should skip these Black Friday deals
 Skip them if your needs are small: phones, a router and a lamp do not need a 1 kWh station. Skip them if you want a whole-home system; those prices depend on the panel and installation, and a percentage off the box matters less than the electrician’s quote. And if you need days of backup with no sun, a fuel generator may still suit you better.
 Frequently asked questions about Black Friday portable power station deals
 When do Black Friday portable power station deals start in 2026? 
 They have already started. EcoFlow’s Early Black Friday sale runs November 2 to 18, Jackery’s Black Friday sale November 4 to 18, BLUETTI’s Early Access November 5 to 18 and Anker’s Early Access November 10 to 18. Black Friday itself is November 27, 2026, and Cyber Monday is November 30.
 Are the Black Friday power station deals real?

 Black Friday power station questions
 When are Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2026?
 Black Friday is Friday, November 27, 2026, and Cyber Monday is Monday, November 30, 2026. Stores often start their sales earlier, and some deals end before the day itself, so every price on this page shows the day we checked it.
 Is the cheapest power station the best deal?
 No. The BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 costs $289.99 and the Dabbsson 600L $299. In independent tests the 600L delivered 653 Wh and the Elite 30 V2 232 Wh, so each usable watt-hour costs $0.46 on the 600L and $1.25 on the Elite 30 V2. The 600L is bigger and heavier (17.6 lb against 9.5 lb), so it isn't the right pick for everyone, but it is the better buy per watt-hour.
 Why don't you show Amazon prices?
 Amazon allows prices only from its own live price feed, and we don't have access to it yet. The Amazon buttons open the listing, where you can see today's price. To compare it with this list, divide the price by the model's usable Wh. Half the models we've priced cost $0.59 or less per usable Wh.
 Are the "regular" prices real?
 We can't tell. Stores set their own regular prices, and we have only recorded prices since early October 2026, so we don't know what each unit usually sells for. That's why we don't show discount percentages. We rank on the price on the day we checked, divided by tested capacity, which works the same whether a unit is on sale or not.
 How often are these prices checked?
 We check each price by hand on the brand's US store, and every card shows the day. The prices on this page were checked on Nov 9, 2026. During the sales, prices and stock can change daily, and some deals need a code at checkout, so check the store before you buy.
 Why isn't a model on this list?
 We rank only models with an independent capacity test and an in-stock store price. When we last checked, the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus, UDPower C600, Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, Oscal PowerMax 2400, Pecron E3600LFP, Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus and EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 were sold out on their brand's US store. The DJI Power 1000 V2 has no US brand-store price we could check, and we can't show Amazon prices. Models without an independent test aren't on our site yet.
 What size power station do I need?
 Add up your devices in our run-time calculator , which uses the same tested capacity as this list. For a refrigerator, our fridge guide has tested run times.
 How do we rank the deals?
 Usable Wh is the middle (median) result of each model's counted independent tests: US units at 120 V,
 AC output, loads of 100 W or more. Across all our models that is 63 tests from 
 9 testers.
 Price is the unit-only price on the brand's US store, in stock, checked by hand on the date shown.
 Where the brand's own store doesn't sell a model, the card names the US dealer we checked.
 Cost per usable Wh is the price divided by usable Wh. Lower is better.
 The verdict is our own rule: Great value at 50¢ or less, Good value up to 60¢, Fair price up to 75¢, Pricey above that.

 Amazon opened its early Black Friday pricing on portable power stations this week, and the cuts run from a 128Wh box that fits in one hand to a 2,080Wh unit built to sit behind the refrigerator. Every discount in this set lands between 34% and 47% off the listing’s regular price, with no coupon or code standing between the reader and the number. Every station here runs a lithium iron phosphate battery, the chemistry that holds up under daily cycling instead of fading after a couple of seasons. Bluetti holds eight of the eleven slots, because that’s where the deep cuts landed this week.
 The list runs in capacity order, smallest first, with the DJI and Anker entries placed where their watt-hours put them. That keeps the price per watt-hour visible as the boxes grow, and the spread runs from 37 cents to just over a dollar. Read the output figure before the capacity figure on every pick, since a big battery behind a small inverter won’t start a kettle.

 Ten stations and one alternator charger, sorted by capacity, each with its own deal box below carrying the live Amazon price and the verified list price it dropped from.

 1 BLUETTI Elite 10 Mini
 The Elite 10 Mini is the smallest real power station in this set, and it gives up almost nothing a desk or a carry-on bag actually asks for. A 200W AC outlet on a 128Wh battery covers a laptop, a camera charger and a drone case on a workday or a travel day, without pretending it belongs under a refrigerator.
 The listing puts that 200W AC outlet beside a 100W USB-C port and DC outputs on a 4.0-pound box measuring 7.8 by 5.7 by 4.3 inches. The LiFePO4 pack is rated past 3,000 cycles, and a 10-millisecond UPS switchover guards the gear sitting on your desk. A built-in light with three modes rides on top, so the box handles the tent and the nightstand too. At 128Wh it falls inside the 100 to 160Wh band airlines allow in the cabin with prior approval, capped at two per passenger.
 It’s a power bank with a wall outlet attached.

 2 BLUETTI Elite 30 Mini
 Bluetti built the Elite 30 Mini around one small idea, trivial until you’ve packed a bag in the dark: a retractable USB-C cable built into the case. It pulls out to charge, then disappears when the job’s done, so the most-forgotten item in portable power stops being a packing step.
 Under the trick sits a 288Wh LiFePO4 battery rated past 6,000 cycles, two AC outlets, two 140W bidirectional USB-C ports, a 30W USB-C port, a USB-A port and a 12V car outlet. The whole layout rides on a 7.3-pound frame, with an outage switchover under 10 milliseconds so a router never notices the grid dropping. Three lighting modes remember your last brightness setting, finishing the grab-and-go case for the hallway closet.
 The built-in cable sells this one.

 3 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2
 Same 288Wh capacity as the Mini above, spent differently. The Elite 30 V2 doubles continuous output to 600W and adds a lifting mode rated at 1,500W, moving a small kettle, a toaster or a CPAP machine from the maybe pile into the covered pile.
 Nine output ports spread across the front of a 9.5-pound box measuring 9.8 by 7 by 6.6 inches. The UPS switchover matches the Mini at 10 milliseconds when the power drops mid-storm and the lights go with it. Bluetti’s UltraCell build keeps standby draw low at 4.5W on DC, so a charged unit in a closet isn’t quietly emptying itself between uses. The fifty dollars over the Mini buys output headroom and nothing else, the right trade when your loads include a heating element.
 Buy this over the Mini for heating loads.

 4 DJI Power 1000 V2
 DJI’s entry is the output bully of the 1kWh class here, rated at 2,600W continuous from a 1,024Wh LFP battery where most rivals stop at 1,800W or less. That headroom covers kettles, power tools and a microwave without tripping the inverter, and at $399.98 it undercuts every other 1kWh station in the roundup.
 Two 140W USB-C ports anchor the front panel, and the case runs as low as 26 decibels in quiet operation. The UPS switchover fires in 10 milliseconds when the grid drops under a desk setup. The catch is printed on the listing itself: the MPPT and car charging modules aren’t built in, so solar or vehicle charging takes a separate DJI adapter that isn’t in the box. Anyone planning a solar-first setup should price that adapter in before calling this the cheap option.

 The Elite 100 Mini stands its kilowatt-hour upright. The tower footprint measures 9.2 by 8.4 inches at the base, so a full 1,004.8Wh of capacity takes less counter, shelf or truck-bed corner than the flat boxes it competes with. It still weighs a manageable 23.5 pounds by the top handle.
 Output is the compromise here, 700W across three AC outlets with a 1,400W surge ceiling, backed by a 140W USB-C port and DC outputs. The UltraCell LiFePO4 pack carries a 6,000-plus cycle rating, the UPS switchover runs at 10 milliseconds, and a built-in light with three modes can light the counter it’s standing on. Shoppers who need a kettle or a microwave running should walk one slot down to the Elite 100 V2 and take its 1,800W instead.

 This is the balanced one in the Bluetti stack, the station in this page’s hero shot, working by the water. A 1,024Wh battery and 1,800W of continuous output with 2,700W of lifting headroom cover the standard camp and outage load list, from the coffee maker to the laptop desk.
 Eleven ports handle the rest of the kit at once, and the LiFePO4 pack is rated past 4,000 cycles. The whole unit weighs 25 pounds in a 12.6 by 8.5 by 9.8 inch case with a hidden handle for one-handed carries. App control over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth covers charging modes, monitoring and firmware from the couch. The UPS switchover holds at 10 milliseconds for the home-office gear it’ll spend most outages protecting. Against the DJI two slots up, it trades raw output for a fuller port spread and built-in charging flexibility.
 The middle of the ladder, done right.

 Anker’s second-generation C1000 pitches its 1,024Wh at the home desk first and the campsite second, and the feature list reads that way from the top. Output peaks higher than the Elite 100 V2 at 2,000W continuous and 3,000W peak across ten ports, giving it the edge when a blender, a kettle and a monitor land on the same strip.
 The app layer is where Anker separates itself here, with a time-of-use mode that schedules charging around peak rates. A 10-millisecond UPS switchover guards the desk while it does so, keeping a dropped grid out of your work. Solar input accepts up to 600W off-grid, the LiFePO4 pack holds at least 80% of its capacity after 4,000 cycles, and the case measures 15.1 by 8.2 by 9.6 inches.  8 DJI Power 2000
 Step up to two kilowatt-hours and the math in this roundup turns in the buyer’s favor as the output figure climbs with the capacity it carries. The DJI Power 2000 carries 2,048Wh of LFP capacity and a 3,000W output rating, the highest continuous figure in this list, at a price that works out near 37 cents per watt-hour.
 Fifteen ports include dual SDC sockets for DJI’s own fast-charge gear, and the case runs as low as 30 decibels. The UPS switchover matches the smaller DJI at 10 milliseconds for home backup duty. Capacity expands with DJI’s 2,048Wh expansion batteries when the base unit stops being enough, though those batteries sell separately. The footprint is a fixed 17.64 by 8.86 by 12.76 inches wherever it lands. The smaller DJI’s adapter caveat applies here in full: MPPT and car charging modules aren’t built in, so solar and vehicle charging need separate DJI adapters.
 Cheapest capacity in the set, full stop.

Price: $749.99 $1,299.00 (save $549.01, 42% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 9 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2
 Bluetti’s big box answers the DJI directly, with 2,080Wh of capacity and 2,600W of continuous output that lifts to 3,900W for loads that surge at startup. It’s the home-backup pick for shoppers who want the charging hardware built in rather than adapted on, since it takes wall, solar and vehicle power through the case.
 The automotive-grade LiFePO4 pack is rated past 6,000 cycles, and standby draw sits at 10W so more of the charge survives to the loads. It can run nine devices at once across its outlet spread, from the fridge circuit to the phone chargers. UPS switchover runs at 15 milliseconds on this model, a step behind the 10-millisecond figure on the smaller Elites, so sensitive desktop setups should note the difference. For fridge, freezer and workshop duty, that gap never enters the conversation.
 Built-in everything, at the big-box price.

 10 BLUETTI FridgePower
 One product in this roundup exists for exactly one job, and it’s shaped like it. The FridgePower packs 2,016Wh and 1,800W of output into a slab just 75 millimeters thin, so it slides into the gap behind the refrigerator or mounts on the kitchen wall.
 Standby draw is the spec that sells a fridge battery, and this one sips 4W at idle where conventional stations burn several times that staying awake. The UPS switchover fires in 10 milliseconds when the grid drops, and the app pushes storm alerts ahead of bad weather. Capacity grows to 8,064Wh as BlueCell 200 expansion batteries stack on, for households that lose power for days at a stretch. A separate glance display comes in the box, so the charge state reads from across the kitchen.
 The fridge gets its own battery now.

Price: $999.00 $1,599.00 (save $600.00, 38% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 11 BLUETTI Charger 1 Alternator Charger (Accessory Pick)
 This one isn’t a power station, and it’s in the roundup because it fixes the weakest link in every station above it. The Charger 1 pulls up to 560W from a vehicle’s alternator while you drive and feeds it to the station in the cargo area. The drive to the trailhead or the cabin stops being dead time for the battery.
 Bluetti rates it for every model in its own line and, by the listing’s count, 95% of third-party power stations, with output adjustable up to 56V. An onboard algorithm watches the vehicle’s starter battery and backs off before the charging load can strand you. An active cooling fan keeps the unit stable in a hot cargo area, and the box includes the 6AWG input cable and installation hardware. It needs a station to feed, which is why it closes the list instead of leading it.
 The road-trip accessory that pays rent.
 BLUETTI Charger 1 
560W alternator charger · 12V/24V input
Price: $218.98 $399.00 (save $180.02, 45% off)
Where to buy: Buy on Amazon 
 How to choose your size
 Match the output figure to the single biggest load first, because a station that can’t start your kettle or your microwave is the wrong station at any capacity. Small boxes under 300W of output belong to phones, laptops, cameras and lights, while the 600W to 2,000W middle covers kitchen and workshop loads one at a time. The 2,600W class and up stops asking which appliance is plugged in.
 Capacity gets cheaper as the boxes get bigger, with the DJI Power 2000 landing near $0.37 per watt-hour while the Elite 30 V2 costs $1.01 for every watt-hour it carries. You’re paying for portability at the small end and getting raw storage at a discount at the big end. Buy the DJI Power 1000 V2 at $399.98 if one box has to split camp and outage duty, and skip the small end entirely if a refrigerator or a heating element is on your list.
 Portable power station deals FAQ
 Are all of these lithium iron phosphate
 Yes, every station in this roundup runs LiFePO4. Cycle ratings on the listings run from 3,000 cycles on the Elite 10 Mini to more than 6,000 on the Elite 30 Mini, Elite 100 Mini and Elite 200 V2. The alternator charger is the exception by design, since it holds no battery of its own.
 Which of these can back up a refrigerator
 The FridgePower is the one built for the job, with its 75mm case shaped for the gap behind the fridge and a 10-millisecond switchover when the grid drops. The two 2kWh stations above it carry the output and capacity for fridge duty as well, and they take the floor space the FridgePower was designed to avoid.
 Do any of these deals need a coupon code
 No, every price in the boxes above is the straight Amazon price on the listing, with no code to enter and no coupon to clip at checkout. The struck-through figure beside each price is that listing’s regular price.

 + We compare today's price with the price the unit actually sold for on most days over the last 90, read by us from the maker's store twice a day. We never use the store's crossed-out "was" price: today 28 of the units we track show one higher than anything we have ever seen them sell for.
 Should I wait for a lower price?
 + Only if today's price is above the price to beat. Discounts are short: of the 78 sales we watched start and finish, half lasted 4 days or less. A unit at its lowest recorded price is unlikely to get much cheaper soon.
 Why is a unit I want missing from the deals?
 + It is at its usual price, out of stock, or too new to judge (we need a few weeks of prices before we know what "usual" is). Every unit we track is in the price-to-beat table with its status.
 Do you earn money from these links?
 + Some stores pay us a commission when you buy through our links, at no cost to you. It never changes the order: deals are ranked by how far each unit is under its own usual price.
 Should I buy on Amazon or from the brand's own store?
 + Either can be cheaper on a given day. Every price on this page is read from the maker's own store, where the "usual" and "lowest" figures come from. If Amazon shows a lower price, check that the unit is sold by Amazon or the brand's official storefront, and compare the return window before you buy.

 + A good price is one under that unit's own price to beat, the lowest we have recorded for it. As a yardstick, the best value on this page today is the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 at $0.46 per watt-hour. Compare dollars per watt-hour only between units of the same battery chemistry.

 The details that decide this purchase
 A power station’s watt-hour rating describes stored energy; its watt rating describes an output limit. A high-output station is not necessarily the longest-running choice for a small router load. Inverter overhead, reserve settings and battery condition all affect delivered energy. Use a manufacturer estimate at a relevant load, then verify the intended setup within the return arrangements.
 A portable station and an IT UPS overlap in some uses but are not interchangeable by default. Check transfer time, automatic restart, low-load timeout and any supported shutdown signalling. The network can remain powered while a NAS still lacks the signal needed to shut down before the battery empties. A USB-C charging socket is not proof of a UPS data interface.
 Compare station-only and solar packages as separate baskets. The panel, cable and adapter must match the station’s input limits. An expansion battery adds stored energy only when it is explicitly supported; it does not automatically increase the inverter’s continuous output. Buy the size and accessories needed for the planned load rather than accepting a bundle because its reference-price saving looks large.
 Plan the energy budget and the next recharge
 Make two lists: equipment that must keep running and equipment that can wait. Record representative watts and the desired duration for each essential load. Multiplying watts by hours gives a preliminary energy requirement, but the station must also cover conversion losses, its own operation and reserve. Treat that calculation as a planning estimate, not a promised runtime. Compare the manufacturer’s relevant test conditions and leave room for battery ageing.
 Keep continuous output, startup demand and stored energy separate. A station may have enough watt-hours for a long light load while failing the starting demand of another appliance. Boost or lifting modes can have restrictions; they should not be substituted for normal rated output without explicit suitability for the device. If your main use is IT equipment, test that particular arrangement rather than inferring compatibility from a kettle demonstration.
 Plan how the station will refill between uses. Check available input power, ventilation, charging-temperature limits and where cables will run. Battery discharge capability in cold weather does not automatically permit charging at the same temperature. Use only the documented operating conditions. A solar panel is an optional source with variable production, not a guarantee that tomorrow’s energy will replace today’s consumption.
 For household circuits or fixed wiring, use the manufacturer’s supported equipment and an appropriate qualified installer. A portable station supplying plug-in equipment is not permission to backfeed a wall outlet. Keep this purchase focused on the supported use you can verify.
 Build a Black Friday price target for the exact purchase
 Create a short comparison record before buying: full model reference, regional version, selected capacity, package contents and seller. Compare recent ordinary selling prices where a reliable history exists, rather than treating a crossed-out reference price as the amount people normally paid. A lower-priced variant in a shared listing is not evidence that the version you want has fallen by the same amount. Record the final selected option and the date of the comparison.
 Set the maximum complete price you would willingly pay for the job described in this guide. Include delivery and any essential cable, adapter or mounting accessory. Compare one suitable alternative at that same complete-price level. If the discounted product still misses a necessary requirement, remove it from the shortlist. A modest reduction on the right configuration can be more useful than a dramatic percentage on an unsuitable one.
 Read the package and seller terms before checkout
 Check whether the offer is new, used, refurbished, an accessory or a complete product. The main image may illustrate a wider system than the selected option includes. Read the package description and confirm the actual seller, delivery estimate and local support route. Keep a copy of the selected reference and invoice so a later warranty or compatibility question can be tied to the product purchased.
 Do not assume a promotion on the manufacturer’s own shop applies to a marketplace seller. Registration requirements, extra coverage and bundle contents can differ. Check the terms shown for the transaction you are making. If an offer is unusually cheap, resolve the model and package difference before interpreting the price as exceptional value.
 Inspect the delivered configuration while problems can be resolved
 At delivery, compare the product label and included parts with the order. Read the supplied installation and operating instructions before connecting equipment. Check for visible damage and use the manufacturer or seller support route if the condition is doubtful. Do not adapt an incorrect regional product merely to avoid returning it.
 Carry out only the setup and checks authorised for that product. Start with a noncritical use of the intended configuration and verify the relevant outputs or communication functions. Keep important work and data protected while checking a new backup arrangement. Record reproducible faults, missing components or mismatched specifications promptly under the seller’s applicable return process. A successful unboxing is not the same as confirming the planned use.

 Buying before the main event can make sense when the exact configuration reaches a documented price target and the seller terms suit the purchase. Waiting may produce a different offer, but neither a later reduction nor continued availability is guaranteed. Avoid buying a second unsuitable product simply to chase a new percentage badge.

A low starting price may belong to a different capacity or incomplete package. Check the seller and the manufacturer’s regional support before treating two offers as equivalent. The recommendation explains which product to investigate; it does not certify stock, an event discount or compatibility with every possible setup.
